holding_summary: A landlord who, on his tenant's failure to pay rent, seized all contents of the premises and, over objection, held the property of the tenant's subtenant on an unfounded suspicion of collusion, is liable in damages to the subtenant for the wrongful seizure.

quotes.text: 2. Landlord and Tenant c&wkey;274(3) — Wrongful Distress — Liability. Where a landlord, on a tenant’s failure to pay rent, seized all the contents of the premises, and against objection of a subtenant held her sewing machine and furniture on unfounded ground that she was in league with tenant, her brother, the subtenant was clearly entitled to compensation for the injury sustained.

She was a subtenant of Desvignes, occupied the upper portion of defendant’s house, and had paid her rent to Desvignes in full up to the time the provisional seizure was obtained and executed by defendant.

notes: Subtenant's occupancy of the upper portion of a house is central to the fact pattern and the court protects her separate property against a landlord's wrongful seizure, implicitly recognizing the subtenancy as lawful; but who_was_letting is the head tenant (a lessee subletting), not an owner-householder, so left unclear, and the court never formally characterizes the arrangement as lease/license/lodging since the dispute is a wrongful-distress tort claim.
Property-damage suit over a gallery destroyed by a runaway motor truck; municipal-nuisance/street-obstruction law, no lodging content.
Jurisdictional dispute over ejectment of a commercial store lessee and tacit reconduction of a store lease; ordinary/yearly commercial lease, not short-term dwelling letting.

holding_summary: Where one, assuming the character of tenant, without the consent of the owner, enters upon premises which are unfit for occupancy and undergoing repairs, including the repairing of plaster upon walls and ceilings saturated and loosened by stormwater, he assumes the risks incidental to such repairs, and, among them, the risk of falling plaster.

notes: Background facts describe an individual owner routinely letting portions of a double tenement cottage to paying tenants by the month as an ordinary matter, unremarked by the court -- consistent with letting as an ordinary incident of ownership; but the actual holding turns on assumption of risk for an unauthorized entrant, not on a formal lease/license characterization, so characterization is left null. Plaintiff's own occupancy at the dwelling in question ran roughly six weeks (mid-November to late December) before the injury, hence 'weeks' rather than the background monthly rental figure.
Year-long residential lease to two co-lessees; dispute is over the several (not solidary) liability of the co-lessees for rent notes, not short-term letting or lodging.
